title: Medical AI: Regulatory history precedes effectiveness evidence
desc: Maps varied specialties and tasks over time while warning that records and versions are not proof of autonomy or improvement.

kps.k: The cluster documents a long regulatory history of medical AI, rather than arguing for its effectiveness or its replacement of professionals.
kps.d: The Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Medical Device List supplies device names, manufacturers, specialty classifications, dates and FDA record links spanning September 1995 to March 2026. This establishes a historical inventory of medical AI products, not their adoption rate, clinical performance or workforce effects. The supplied material presents no competing argumentative positions.

kps.k: Medical AI encompasses different specialties and tasks; the inventory does not establish a common level of autonomy.
kps.d: Radiology features prominently, alongside cardiovascular, ophthalmic, neurological and other classifications. Products include tools for reconstruction, segmentation, triage, quantification, planning and monitoring. This diversity supports analysing particular applications rather than treating medical AI as one capability. Product names and listing metadata alone do not show whether systems augment clinicians or replace their judgment.

kps.k: Successive product records should not count automatically as distinct technologies or evidence of improvement.
kps.d: The list traces AutoContour from a 2020 entry through later RADAC versions, including V5 in March 2026. These records document a product family's regulatory history, but do not independently establish technical novelty, performance gains or wider deployment. Analyses of growth should distinguish record counts from product families and version changes.

kps.k: Regulatory links make the inventory a starting point for due diligence, not a substitute for clinical evidence.
kps.d: Entries link to 510(k), De Novo and premarket-approval records, including approval supplements. Those pathways provide traceability but should not be conflated. Assessing intended use, safety, accuracy, clinical benefit or deployment requires examining the underlying reviews and additional evidence; the supplied extracts contain listing metadata rather than those findings.

vlens.an: The regulatory-source evidence supports the proposition descriptively rather than through an explicit argument. The FDA inventory establishes a long regulatory history across specialties, tasks and pathways, while the supplied material contains no clinical-effectiveness findings, adoption measures, autonomy assessments or workforce-replacement evidence. It also substantiates the cluster’s caution against treating every regulatory record as a distinct technology or demonstrated improvement, because the same product family reappears in successive versions. Material variation lies in device type, specialty, task, date and regulatory pathway—not in competing views about effectiveness. Because the curated evidence contains only this inventory, no broader position should be attributed to regulators, courts or professional bodies generally.

elens.an: The sole curated source for the 2026 period supports the proposition by functioning as a regulatory inventory rather than evidence of effectiveness, clinical adoption, autonomy or professional replacement. Its records span from 1995 to 2026 and cover multiple specialties and task types, supporting the cluster’s treatment of medical AI as a heterogeneous set of applications with a long regulatory history. It also traces successive versions within product families—most clearly AutoContour/RADAC—supporting the warning that additional regulatory records should not automatically be interpreted as distinct technologies or demonstrated improvement. There is no substantive internal disagreement because the source does not advance competing arguments; the material variation is instead descriptive, across dates, specialties, tasks and regulatory pathways. The inventory’s FDA links improve traceability but do not themselves supply comparative safety, accuracy, clinical-benefit or deployment evidence. Because this is one curated inventory, its alignment should not be generalized to other regulators, clinicians, manufacturers or researchers.

parents.t: Medical AI device inventories: regulatory breadth does not establish innovation or impact
